title: A Person Who Changed My Life
paragraphs: Every student who has spent time at WKU can name at least one person who changed the way they thought about themselves. For Kamila Seitkali, that person is not a professor, not a famous writer, and not a historical figure. It is a quiet woman called Apai Zarina, who worked in the WKU library for thirty-seven years and retired the spring before Kamila arrived.

Kamila never met Apai Zarina in person. But she met her in the catalogue — in the handwritten notes that Zarina had left in the margins of dozens of library books over the decades. They were small observations: a phrase that reminded her of a song, a fact that connected two different subjects, a question that the text had raised but not answered. "She left a trail," Kamila says. "Like a thread through the library. I kept finding her notes in books I was reading for completely different reasons."

The notes were never signed. Kamila only discovered who had written them after asking the librarian who had worked alongside Zarina for twenty years. "There was a woman who did that," the librarian told her. "She said books were a conversation, and you had to reply." Kamila found this idea extraordinary. The books that Zarina had annotated were not books that anyone asked her to read. They were books that she had chosen herself, over a lifetime of curious reading.

What struck Kamila most was the quality of the attention. The notes were not summaries. They were responses — personal, specific, and intellectually alive. In one book about Central Asian history, Zarina had written: "This paragraph contradicts what Auezov says on page 218 of his collection. Look it up." In a linguistics textbook, she had written: "The author has not read Saussure carefully enough." These were the responses of someone who read with enormous concentration and no deference to authority.

Kamila began to model her own reading on Zarina's. She started writing in the margins of her own books — not to summarise, but to respond. She asked questions. She made connections. She disagreed. "It changed everything," she says. "Reading stopped being a passive activity where I received information. It became a dialogue. I became a person who talks back to texts."

"There's something important about people who do their work quietly, without recognition," Kamila wrote in her journal. "Apai Zarina spent thirty-seven years adding her voice to books that no one was watching. She didn't do it for credit. She did it because she believed that ideas deserve a response." Kamila has since started her own habit: whenever she finishes a book, she writes one sentence in the margin. Not a summary. A reply.

She has never discovered what happened to Apai Zarina after her retirement. She may still be living in Uralsk, in a flat that is full of books and notes. She may be reading right now, annotating something, carrying on the conversation that she started decades before Kamila was born.

Some people change your life by being in it. Others change it by leaving something behind. Apai Zarina belongs to the second kind — the rare and beautiful people who improve the world they live in simply by paying attention.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Do you have a person who changed the way you think? Not a celebrity or a philosopher — just someone real.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Apai Raushan, definitely. The woman I met on the train to Almaty. She saw something in me I couldn't see myself.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Mine is someone I never met — a librarian who left notes in books. She taught me how to read.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: A person who taught you through their absence. That's a beautiful kind of influence.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I think the people who change us most are often the ones who ask us to pay attention differently.

dialogue.speaker: Rustam
dialogue.text: Or the ones who show us that something we took for granted — like a train journey — can be extraordinary.

keyPhrases.context: "Books that Zarina had annotated." = books she had written notes in.
"She read with no deference to authority." = she questioned experts.
"She left a trail." — a series of clues or marks to follow.
"She left notes in the margins." = in the blank spaces at the edges of pages.
"Reading stopped being a passive activity." — something you just receive.
"People who improve the world simply by paying attention."
"Carrying on the conversation that she started decades before."
"People who do their work quietly, without recognition."

vocab.definition: to add notes or comments to a text
vocab.example: Apai Zarina annotated dozens of library books over her thirty-seven years.

vocab.definition: respectful submission to the opinion of someone else
vocab.example: She read with no deference to authority — she questioned everything.

vocab.definition: very unusual or remarkable; beyond what is ordinary
vocab.example: Kamila found the idea of books as conversations extraordinary.

vocab.definition: to say the opposite of something else; to be in conflict
vocab.example: "This paragraph contradicts what Auezov says." — she found a disagreement.

vocab.definition: something that connects parts of a story or situation; a strand
vocab.example: "She left a trail — like a thread through the library." — a connecting path.

vocab.definition: a conversation between two people; an exchange of ideas
vocab.example: "Reading became a dialogue." — an active exchange rather than passive receiving.

vocab.definition: acknowledgement of something or someone's achievements
vocab.example: She did her work "without recognition" — no one credited or noticed her.

vocab.definition: the power to have an effect on someone or something
vocab.example: Apai Zarina's influence on Kamila was lasting — changing how she reads.
